stimulus.text:
“Give me your tired, your poor,
Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free,
The wretched refuse of your teeming shore.
Send these, the homeless, tempest-tost to me,
I lift my lamp beside the golden door!”

Emma Lazarus, “The New Colossus” (1883), written for the Statue of Liberty.
stimulus.source_note: Emma Lazarus, “The New Colossus” (1883). Public domain.

books.section: Topic 6.8 Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age

stem: The poem’s welcome contrasts most directly with which development of the same decade?

options.text: The opening of Ellis Island in 1892
options.misconception: Picks a later event that received immigrants instead of excluding them.

options.text: The founding of Hull House in 1889
options.misconception: Confuses a settlement house that helped immigrants with a law that excluded them.

options.text: The growth of ethnic neighborhoods in cities
options.misconception: Treats where immigrants lived as a contradiction of the welcome.

rationales.A: Ellis Island opened in 1892, in the next decade, and it received immigrants rather than excluding them.
rationales.B: The poem, written in 1883, welcomes all the poor, while the 1882 act shut out Chinese laborers by nationality.
rationales.C: Hull House aided immigrants. It did not contradict the poem’s welcome.
rationales.D: Ethnic neighborhoods show immigrants settling together. They do not contradict the welcome.
rationales.general:
Match the poem’s welcome against a law from the same years.
1. The poem welcomes the poor of every land, without exception.
2. The 1882 act shut out Chinese laborers because of their nationality.
3. A welcome for all and a ban on one group point in opposite directions.
4. Ellis Island and Hull House both fit the welcome, so they do not contrast with it.
Remember: a contrast needs two things that pull in opposite directions.
